title: Texas Autonomous Trucking: Match the Operator to the Work
seoTitle: Texas Autonomous Trucking Operators and Commercial Service 2026
subtitle: A buyer’s comparison of driverless service, supervised customer freight and future launches across Texas trucking operations.
seoDescription: Compare Aurora, Kodiak, Torc, Waabi, Gatik, Bot Auto, PlusAI and Einride in Texas: current operating evidence, service boundaries and freight buyer questions.
author: Sulayman Bowles
evidenceBoundary: Reviewed October 12, 2026. This is a selected comparison of documented Texas freight programs, not an exhaustive census or safety ranking. Operating milestones and performance figures are attributed to their issuers. A driverless customer load, an observer-supported run, closed-course validation, a responder plan and future capacity are separate evidence. Public reports do not establish the reader’s price, accepted lane, reserved truck or contractual service level.
content: Texas autonomous trucking is already a purchasing question, but the useful unit is a defined freight job. A retailer replenishing stores in Dallas–Fort Worth, a sand supplier serving Permian well sites and a carrier covering I-45 need different vehicles, endpoints and support. Grouping them under one driverless-truck headline conceals the conditions that decide whether a service can move the buyer’s goods.

At the October 12, 2026 cutoff, Aurora reports commercial driverless freight on public roads; Gatik identifies operating driverless regional networks; and Bot Auto has documented a paid Houston–Hutchins load with nobody in the cab. Other important programs retain onboard personnel or describe a future driver-out launch. The task is to match each statement to its route and operating role before assigning capacity. [Aurora October update](#source-aurora-october); [Gatik regional operations](#source-gatik-pepsico); [Bot Auto commercial load](#source-bot-commercial).

A qualified shortlist starts with evidence of the required operation, then moves to a dated service proposal. A company can be technically advanced and commercially unsuitable for a particular shipment. It can also provide useful supervised freight service without meeting a buyer’s requirement for a driverless operation.

sections.title: Read the operating stage before the company name
paragraphs: The table separates eight participants with concrete Texas evidence. It describes the reviewed program, not every vehicle an operator owns. Where a statement remains a target, keep that condition in the capacity plan. An announced commercial relationship is useful discovery evidence; it is not a reservation for your next outbound load.

The dates matter because a new platform can change the onboard role while other platforms remain in a different stage. Aurora’s second-generation explanation and Kodiak’s new Laredo customer announcement show why a generic statement about a company being driverless can be too broad. [Aurora platform explanation](#source-aurora-faq); [Kodiak Laredo operation](#source-kodiak-charger).

sections.title: Aurora: current driverless operation needs a platform and endpoint
paragraphs: Aurora’s July 22 explanation says its second-generation International LT trucks operate with an empty driver’s seat. Some trips may carry roadside-assistance staff in a rear seat; Aurora expressly says that person neither drives nor supervises the driving. Record the role accurately. An empty driver seat establishes something different from a guarantee that every trip has an empty cab. [July launch explanation](#source-aurora-faq).

Its July 29 shareholder letter describes deployed driverless operations between Detmar’s Midland facility and Capital Sand’s Monahans mining site along I-20. The letter separately labels fueling and weigh-station work as supervised testing. That distinction matters when a proposed lane depends on those activities. Ask for the exact released configuration instead of extending one successful capability to every stop. [Customer endpoint and support-stage evidence, pages 7–8](#source-aurora-q2).

The October 8 update reports more than 500,000 driverless miles since commercial launch. That is a company-reported accumulated operating measure, not a count of available trucks or evidence that an unreviewed customer yard is supported. Treat it as experience to investigate, then request lane-specific acceptance and dispatch terms. [October update](#source-aurora-october).

sections.title: Kodiak: keep the industrial and highway files separate
paragraphs: Kodiak’s September 25 release reports 35 Atlas-owned driverless trucks and more than 40,000 cumulative paid driverless hours as of June 30. Atlas’s July 31 announcement adds a second load-out point on its Dune Express system, while targeting public-road operation for early 2027 subject to operational and regulatory milestones. Those industrial deliveries should not populate the spreadsheet cell for current driverless I-45 capacity. [Industrial operating measures](#source-kodiak-highway); [Atlas expansion boundaries](#source-kodiak-atlas).

The same September release describes daily Dallas–Houston preparation deliveries with a safety observer and closed-course driverless validation. An observer not touching the wheel during a run is not evidence that the public-road service has removed that observer. Unsupervised highway launch remains targeted for the end of 2026. [Highway preparation](#source-kodiak-highway).

The October 8 Charger announcement is even more explicit: Dallas–Laredo customer loads have a safety driver behind the wheel. Its 96% Autonomy Readiness Measure at September-end describes materially completed safety-case claims and evidence. It does not mean 96% route availability, 96% autonomous miles or a 96% chance of a completed launch. [Current Charger operation and metric definition](#source-kodiak-charger).

sections.title: Gatik and Bot Auto answer different freight questions
paragraphs: Gatik’s January disclosure identifies driverless Dallas–Fort Worth operations using 26- and 30-foot trucks between distribution facilities and stores. The June PepsiCo announcement identifies existing driverless operations across Texas, Arizona and Arkansas. This is a regional replenishment proposition: stop frequency, vehicle capacity, temperature needs and receiving access can matter more than a long-haul terminal map. [Vehicle and regional scope](#source-gatik-driverless); [PepsiCo operating statement](#source-gatik-pepsico).

The August 25 update reports 85,000 completed driverless orders and 99% on-time delivery across Gatik’s operations. Those are issuer-reported network measures, not Texas-only observations or a matched comparison with another company. Its contracted-revenue figure also differs from recognized revenue and cash received. Request the period, accepted-load denominator, cancellation treatment and route-level record relevant to your stores. [Latest reviewed operating update](#source-gatik-august).

Bot Auto’s April 30 company release documents a 230-mile commercial load from northeast Houston to Hutchins, booked through Ryan Transportation, without an onboard safety driver, observer or dependence on low-latency remote human feedback. That is a concrete completed shipment. The issuer’s cost and profitability language does not supply an independently reviewed cost ledger or a shipper tariff. Its current site provides a freight inquiry path; current recurring capacity still needs a proposal. [Dated commercial load](#source-bot-commercial); [Current company overview](#source-bot-current).

sections.title: Waabi and PlusAI: live freight with an onboard boundary
paragraphs: Waabi and Volvo’s October 5 Warp launch brings the Volvo VNL Autonomous into Dallas–Houston customer operations, including direct deliveries to third-party facilities in an LTL network. The release says current hauls have an observer in the driver’s seat. Preserve that exact wording; it neither proves the observer never intervenes nor establishes driverless service. Direct facility access and the onboard role are separate buying attributes. [Warp release](#source-waabi-warp).

International and Ryder’s March 31 PlusAI trial places factory-integrated SuperDrive on a live Laredo–Temple lane. The release reports 92% autonomous route coverage supervised by a human safety driver and inspection below 30 minutes in the pilot. A coverage percentage cannot establish driver removal; an inspection KPI cannot set a universal allowance for a different truck, trailer or facility. [Pilot facts and qualifications](#source-international-ryder). PlusAI’s September 3 release continues to target a 2027 commercial launch of factory-built autonomous trucks; keep that target separate from the present trial. [Current commercialization roadmap](#source-plus-roadmap).

For a buyer evaluating these programs, ask what is being purchased today and what would change at driver-out transition: contract price, liability allocation, onboarding work, route restrictions, staffing and fallback service. Keep today’s freight option available for evaluation while excluding forecast labor removal from the current savings case.

sections.title: Torc and Einride: preparation is useful evidence with limits
paragraphs: Torc’s February 2026 update describes established Dallas–Fort Worth testing and a fleet operations facility. Its production-platform article separates driver-out validation on a closed multi-lane track from Fort Worth operations and a 2027 market-entry roadmap. Closed-track validation is important technical work, but it does not demonstrate an unsupervised customer run on the buyer’s highway lane. [Current-year testing description](#source-torc-2026); [Platform and roadmap](#source-torc-roadmap).

Einride’s March 17 memorandum with SH 130 Concession Company describes a validation testbed on Segments 5 and 6 and plans for frontage-road connectivity. The March 24 release reports NHTSA approval and an Austin cabless demonstration explicitly belonging to an R&D project. The reviewed releases do not provide a bookable Texas commercial lane or the underlying approval instrument. [Testbed memorandum](#source-einride-testbed); [Austin research demonstration](#source-einride-austin).

These programs may justify technical diligence, facility discussions or a future option. Tie any capacity commitment to named release conditions and a delivery date the counterparty will actually support. A press-event vehicle, a future manufacturing program and a service slot should remain different entries.

sections.title: Use an evidence ladder without turning it into a safety ranking
paragraphs: Texas DPS publishes first-responder interaction plans for these and additional organizations, including Stack, Fountainhead Logistics and International Transport Engineering. That is a useful discovery route for responder information. Posting a plan alone does not establish a permit, passenger access, a commercial truck lane or a complete Texas operator census. [DPS plan directory](#source-dps-plans).

The following ladder is a purchasing framework. Movement requires evidence of the particular work, rather than a larger generic autonomous-mile total. A service can be commercially relevant at several stages; the buyer should know which stage it is paying for.

sections.title: Ask for comparable service evidence
paragraphs: NHTSA warns that crash-reporting data are not normalized for vehicle miles, fleet exposure or operating domain and can include incomplete information and duplicates. Raw report counts cannot support a safety league table. Different goods, roads, weather and supervision also complicate comparisons between operator disclosures. [NHTSA data limitations](#source-nhtsa-method).

For service performance, define accepted loads, completed loads, cancellations, arrival-window rules and recovery events before comparing percentages. Ask whether on-time reporting excludes rejected loads or stops outside the supported domain. Measure from ready freight at origin to accepted delivery, so a fast highway run cannot hide a missed dock window or terminal wait.

Also identify the contracting carrier, technology provider, truck owner and responder. Driver-as-a-Service and Transportation-as-a-Service describe different allocations of work; the label alone cannot settle inspection, maintenance, cargo custody or exception costs. A buyer needs an accountable operating arrangement, not only an autonomous-driving capability.

sections.title: A buyer file that can support the first lane
paragraphs: Build one file for the actual proposed operation. These recommendations follow from the stage comparison; they are not claims that each operator requires identical terminals or commercial terms.
bullets: Name the origin, destination, gates, docks, intermediate stops, equipment, commodity and delivery windows; ask which are accepted today.
Record the exact truck platform and every onboard or remote role, including who can control driving and who provides roadside support.
Separate supervised freight, driverless customer work, closed-course testing and conditional launch dates in the capacity plan.
Obtain a price and responsibility schedule covering loading, inspection, release, maintenance, fuel, recovery, custody and backup capacity.
Request recent lane-specific accepted-load and exception records with definitions, and confirm the applicable authority and insurance evidence.
Approve expansion against completed deliveries and resolved operational conditions rather than fleet forecasts or unmatched safety totals.

sections.title: Update the comparison when the operating boundary changes
paragraphs: Revisit Kodiak’s highway rows when a dated release confirms driver-out customer operation, and revisit Waabi, PlusAI and Torc when their disclosed onboard role or commercial stage changes. Revisit Einride when Texas evidence moves from demonstration/testbed to a specified customer operation. Retain the prior stage so a forecast becoming an observation remains visible.

For an existing lane, a new endpoint, platform, trailer, weather restriction or support arrangement can matter more than another national milestone. Reconfirm availability and contractual responsibility before increasing volume. The most useful Texas trucking update is the one that tells the reader which freight job has become usable, and what evidence still stands between that development and a purchase.

faqs.question: Which autonomous truck operators have documented driverless freight in Texas?
faqs.answer: The reviewed evidence identifies Aurora public-road driverless freight, Gatik regional operations including Texas, and Bot Auto’s dated Houston–Hutchins commercial load. Kodiak also has Atlas-owned Permian industrial driverless deliveries. These different domains do not establish open service for every shipper or an exhaustive census. [Aurora](#source-aurora-october); [Gatik](#source-gatik-pepsico); [Bot Auto](#source-bot-commercial); [Atlas](#source-kodiak-atlas).

faqs.question: Is Kodiak’s Dallas–Houston or Dallas–Laredo service driverless?
faqs.answer: At the October 12 cutoff, the September 25 release still targets unsupervised Dallas–Houston highway service by year-end. The October 8 Charger Dallas–Laredo release explicitly has a safety driver behind the wheel. Industrial Permian driverless operation is a separate program. [Highway launch preparation](#source-kodiak-highway); [Charger operation](#source-kodiak-charger).

faqs.question: Are Waabi’s new Volvo trucks running without an onboard observer?
faqs.answer: The October 5 Warp release describes current Dallas–Houston autonomous customer hauls with an observer in the driver’s seat. Direct delivery to third-party facilities does not remove that qualification. [Volvo–Waabi customer-operation release](#source-waabi-warp).

faqs.question: Can autonomous miles or NHTSA crash counts identify the safest freight provider?
faqs.answer: The reviewed disclosures and raw crash counts do not support that ranking. NHTSA says incident totals are not normalized for fleet, mileage or domain, and reporting visibility varies. Request a safety case and relevant operating evidence, with comparable definitions and exposure. [NHTSA methodology](#source-nhtsa-method).
